title: Commit .terraform.lock.hcl for both tofu environments
description:
No .terraform.lock.hcl exists anywhere in the repo, so a bare `tofu init` resolves the provider constraint to whatever is newest. The plan reviewed on a PR need not be the plan the merge applies, and on an adoption apply that is the difference between "adopt" and "replace" — a provider minor can change a CustomizeDiff.

Mitigated for now by pinning both environments to an exact version (6.66.0, the newest stable 6.x as of 2026-09-28) instead of `~> 6.0`. That removes the resolution drift but not the weaker guarantee: a version pin has no hashes, so it does not protect against a republished artifact, and it has to be bumped by hand.

The real fix needs tofu present, which this session did not have:

    cd terraform/environments/staging && tofu providers lock \
      -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64
    # same for production, commit both .terraform.lock.hcl files

then add `-lockfile=readonly` to the init in the Staging, Staging Plan, Production and Production Plan workflows so CI fails rather than silently resolving something else. Do not add that flag before the lockfiles are committed — init fails without one.

Found by the import-blast-radius pass on PR #248 (P1), which is also the reviewer the 2026-09-18 census proposed and this repo did not yet have. Worth adding .reviewers/import-blast-radius.md so it is not briefed inline next time.
notes:
DONE for the mitigation part, and the instruction below is now stale. Both .terraform.lock.hcl are committed (tofu 1.9.0, -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64, aws 6.66.0 with h1: and zh: hashes) and all five tofu init calls across the four workflows pass -lockfile=readonly. The description says not to add that flag before the lockfiles exist; they exist, so it is added.

An independent regeneration by the import-blast-radius reviewer produced a byte-identical file, and it tested the guard in both directions: a widened constraint still installs the LOCKED version rather than the newest satisfying one, and a constraint bumped past the lock fails init with "must use tofu init -upgrade". One qualification it measured: readonly *warns* rather than fails on a missing platform hash, so "the checksums are fixed" is slightly stronger than the mechanism — both platforms are present here, so it does not bite.

What remains, and why this stays open rather than closing: bumping the provider now needs `tofu providers lock` run deliberately in both directories, and nothing enforces that the two environments stay on the same version. Worth a line in CLAUDE.md or a CI check that diffs the two lockfiles.

title: [guided builds] The guide page
description: Frontend for one guide: the steps, the recommended parts with thumbnails, the change affordances for each refinement, the resulting parts list with STL links, and a shareable URL encoding the selections. Watch out: use-url-parameters.ts and use-blueprint-url-cleanup.ts rewrite the query string after load, so guide state must not be silently stripped the way blueprint deep links were (see the environment banner, which captures the arrival URL in a lazy useState initializer for exactly this reason).
notes:
Constraint from the API (openforge_catalog-anc, PR #240): /api/guides/<key>/resolve refuses a query key it does not recognise, with a 400. So the page must build the API query from the step keys the guide document defines, NOT by forwarding window.location.search — otherwise a shared link that has been through Facebook or a campaign tracker arrives carrying fbclid or utm_source and the person sees an error instead of their build. The API stays strict on purpose: ignoring unknown keys would make a typo'd selection resolve silently against the wrong state.

Also from that PR: every image in a resolved part now carries image_type, so the page can tell a thumbnail from a documentation image rather than taking the first image it is handed.

Watch out for image_type when you use it. Exactly one place in the backend reads it — _get_blueprint_thumbnail, with a .get, so nothing notices if the filter stops matching — and four call sites in blueprints.py return it to clients unread, which is what makes it part of the published shape of a blueprint's image object rather than something a test can see. A reviewer measured that removing the column from both image queries leaves the full suite at its exact baseline. So whatever the guide page does with image_type should be the first thing that actually proves the field works end to end, and should come with a test that fails if the column stops being projected.
close_reason: Merged as PR #241 (squash b9d6472) into test. The guide page, the four format terms, three parser bugs it surfaced, and thirteen rounds of review. Forced because the only blocker is its own parent epic openforge_catalog-2i5, which stays open until the remaining slices land. Follow-ups filed rather than carried: openforge_catalog-kv8 (the release rule written twice across the Python/TS seam — the class behind four of round 13's five findings), -url (a pinned part gives no sign it is retired), -lfi (wire /guides into the nav), -dpo, -tw3, -1rh (a11y), -hqw (complexity queue, re-measured), -6d6 (ruff pin).

title: Bound the API pool's connect wait so an idle-hour cold start fails visibly
description:
Staging Aurora runs at min_capacity 0 with a one-hour auto-pause, and a resume from zero takes about 20 s (measured: seven cold starts on 2026-09-27 converging on a cluster CloudWatch shows at 0.0 ACU, durations 20.1/20.0/18.3/10.8/10.2/9.3/9.2 s, all ENDing within 3 s of each other).

The API function has timeout = 30 and builds a psycopg_pool ConnectionPool whose default timeout is also 30. Those two deadlines are the same instant, so the first request after an idle period dies as `Task timed out` with no exception and no traceback — the pool caught the ConnectionTimeout, logged a WARNING, and rescheduled, and then the function wall arrived before the pool gave the caller anything.

The cheap, bounded fix is a pool timeout below the function budget — `ConnectionPool(url, timeout=20)` in openforge/db/__init__.py — so that request fails as a logged PoolTimeout with a stack trace, and the next one succeeds because the cluster is up by then.

What NOT to do, both checked:
- Raising the Lambda timeout past 30 s buys nothing. CloudFront reaches the ALB with OriginReadTimeout: 30 (distribution E1C2HQJ3R98WNB), so the browser path gives up at 30 s regardless; a larger function budget relocates the failure to a CloudFront 504 and would need a matching change in openforge-infra-frontend to mean anything.
- A non-zero min_capacity removes the wait but costs roughly 0.5 ACU continuously to rescue one request per idle period. Wrong trade for staging on a Patreon budget.

Not done in PR #248: it is a code change to shared connection handling, not a staging-parity change, and the serverless-architecture reviewer raised then withdrew the timeout half of it there with the CloudFront evidence above.

title: [test] global.fetch mocks are never restored, and the cleanup has a 68-test blast radius
description:
`jest.config.js` sets no `restoreMocks`, `resetMocks` or `clearMocks`, and `src/test-utils/setup.ts` touches only `console`. jsdom supplies no `global.fetch`, so a test that assigns one leaves it assigned for the rest of its file. `afterEach(() => jest.restoreAllMocks())` does not help: `global.fetch = jest.fn()` is an assignment, not a spy, so `restoreAllMocks` never touches it.

Nothing is riding on it today — every test in the files that assign a fetch arranges its own, confirmed with `npx jest --randomize` over three seeds — and each file gets its own environment, so nothing crosses files. The risk is latent: a future test that forgets to arrange one would silently inherit its neighbour's, and the suite would not notice.

The obvious fix — restore the ambient global in a global `afterEach` in `setup.ts` — **must not be shipped as-is.** Measured by test-coverage-reviewer in round 2 of PR #246: it puts five unrelated suites at **68 failures** (`blueprint-store`, `tag-store`, `image-gallery`, `admin-context`, `admin-page`). Those tests install one mock in the describe body and use `mockResolvedValueOnce` per test, which is a legitimate file-scoped pattern that still works under `jest -t`. So the probe is wrong about them, not the reverse.

Whoever takes this should expect to convert those five suites to per-test arrangement first, or find a narrower guard that only catches the inheriting case. Deliberately not bundled into a page redesign.

title: PartSelectionModal is not a dialog: no role, no aria-modal, no focus trap, no Escape, no focus restoration
description:
Found by frontend-conventions-reviewer while reviewing PR #241, and deliberately **not** filed as a finding on that PR: it is pre-existing, the same modal is used by the blueprint page (`src/components/blueprint/config-box.tsx`), and filing it there would have been manufacturing a finding on a PR that only reuses the component. Agreed out of scope there; captured here so it does not evaporate for having been found in the wrong review.

`src/components/part-selection-modal.tsx` is 83 lines and its only accessibility-relevant line is `createPortal`. Verified at `ca19f63`: no `role="dialog"`, no `aria-modal`, no `aria-labelledby`, no focus trap, no Escape handler, no focus restoration to the control that opened it. It renders as a portal behind a `fixed; inset: 0` overlay, so a screen-reader or keyboard user gets a portal with no announced role, Tab walks out of it into the page behind, and Escape does nothing.

Two consumers, so fixing it once fixes both surfaces:

- `src/components/guides/guide-parts.tsx` (the guide page's part inspector)
- `src/components/blueprint/config-box.tsx` (the blueprint page)

Minimum shape: `role="dialog"` + `aria-modal="true"` + `aria-labelledby` pointing at its own heading, an Escape keydown that calls the existing close path, focus moved into the dialog on open, and focus restored to the opener on close. A focus trap is the largest piece; the other four are small.

Related, from the same review (react-hooks-reviewer on 4117785889): the overlay's unreachability is currently load-bearing elsewhere. `GuidePage` does not clear `inspecting` when a role leaves the resolution, and `blueprint-context.tsx:88`'s guard leans on `initialMd5` never changing under a live store; both claims hold only because the questions behind the modal cannot be clicked while it is open. If this modal ever becomes dismissible-but-mounted, both come due together.

title: [openforge-infra] Deploy roles can overwrite the baseline's tofu lock row
description:
`state_guard` in `terraform/modules/github-oidc` denies `dynamodb:DeleteTable` and `dynamodb:UpdateTable` on the lock table, and the module comment claims "apps can never write baseline state". That is true for the state OBJECTS and false for the LOCK: all four backends share `openforge-infra-tfstate-lock`, and `PowerUserAccess` grants `dynamodb:*`, so item-level writes are allowed. A deploy role can drop or overwrite the row that represents the baseline holding its own lock.

Pre-existing — autoblender has had this since #5 and the production catalog since the start. openforge-infra#8 adds a second holder, which is what surfaced it.

Suggested fix is a `dynamodb:LeadingKeys` condition scoping each app to its own `LockID` values, rather than a blanket item-level Deny, which would break the app locking its own state.

Found by the terraform-reviewer on openforge-infra#8 (P3, not blocking).

title: Guides: blame can name a question the wizard has not reached
description:
From round 7 of PR #241 (silent-failure-hunter, flagged inside thread 4115823431 as belonging to another reviewer's lane).

In the state where a step answer empties a part, the blame can name a question that _up_to_first_unanswered has cut from the step list -- so the page shows a reason pointing at a question that is not on screen.

Reproduced with the real fixture at method=wall-on-tile&size=4x1&connectors=side-dragonlock: both method and size come back with their selected answer in `unavailable` and a `because` entry naming `connectors`, which the wizard has not reached.

PR #241 made the state legible (a folded step and a folded refinement both now carry their reason), so this is the remaining half: either the reason should name only questions currently on screen, or the page should be able to reveal the one it names.

title: Rotate the R2 credentials once the hand-built staging Lambda is retired
description:
`Openforge-Catalog-API` in staging carries live plaintext `CLOUDFLARE_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `CLOUDFLARE_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `SECRET_KEY` and `API_TOKEN` in its function configuration, and a literal `PGPASSWORD`. Its replacement (`openforge-catalog-api`, PR #248) sources all of them from Secrets Manager instead.

Nothing is known to have leaked — a function environment is readable only by principals with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration on it — but those values have sat in a hand-edited config for nine months, staging and production share the R2 bucket, and the same credentials appear in a local `.env`. Once `openforge_catalog-rc2` deletes the old function, rotating the R2 pair costs little and closes the window.

Order matters: rotate after the new function is serving and the old one is gone, and update the app secret in both accounts plus any local `.env` in the same pass, or the catalog loses its object store.

Noted by the terraform-reviewer while reading openforge-infra#8.

title: Epic: guided builds — tell people how to make a wall
description: The catalog is good at finding a named piece and bad at telling someone what to print. Invert the blueprint: instead of a part declaring what it accepts, a guide declares a thing you want to build and the parts that make it, driven by data rather than code. First slice is 'how do I make a wall?' end to end, covering build|s2w, build|wall on tile and build|separate wall. Design, with the verified state of the existing data model, is docs/design/guided-builds.md. Decisions already taken with Devon on 2026-09-19: guides are repo fixtures loaded into a table (admin editor later); the output is a parts list with downloads plus a shareable URL; wall only for the first slice; and the synthesised base slot comes out of the parser. The reason for that last one was first written as 'connection|openforge already implies a base', which review proved false across the catalog — 4,368 records carry the tag and only 2,455 have a base slot. The true rule is per method: within build|separate wall the slot and the tag are the same fact (1,220 of 1,221 openforge walls, and none of the 115 separate-wall floors), within build|thick wall likewise for the openforge walls carrying component|wall (87 of 100). Where the base goes is also per method and is NOT 'under the floor' in general: separate wall puts it under the wall, wall on tile under the floor (295 floors, no walls), s2w with the wall (no s2w floor carries a slot; the composition blueprints put fulfills: base on the wall part), and s-system nowhere. Any UI that replaces the synthesised slot has to read the build method, not just the connection tag. Feature slots (door, torch, lintel...) stay and are a later phase, so the model must not preclude them.
notes: Where the base goes is per method and is not 'under the floor' in general (PR #238 round 5): separate wall puts it under the wall (1,220 of 1,221 openforge walls carry the slot, 0 of 115 floors), wall on tile under the floor (295 floors, no walls), s2w with the wall (no s2w floor carries a slot; the composition blueprints put fulfills: base on the wall part), and s-system nowhere. Any UI that replaces the synthesised slot has to read the method.

title: [catalog] Make 'Select This Part' a button, not a link
description:
User feedback, 2026-09-30, on the part selection dialog: 'Recommendation for the UI when selecting a part: Make "Select This Part" a big colored button that screams click me! instead of a link.'

In the part detail pane it currently renders as an underlined text link, sitting immediately beside '(Report Issue with this model)' in the same weight and colour. The primary action and a secondary reporting link are visually identical, and the primary one is the entire reason the dialog is open.

Make it a filled button, sized and coloured as a primary action, clearly separated from the report link. The report link can stay a link - that is the right weight for it.

Worth noting this dialog is reached from the guided builds flow as well as from browsing, so it is on the path of the feature that just shipped.

title: [guides] wall.yaml's with-base options let you browse to a tile that already is a base
description:
Found by the guide-semantics reviewer on PR #253, where the same defect was inherited and then fixed in the new floor guide. wall.yaml still has it.

wall.yaml:200-206 (and the floor-print with-base option) puts NO connector constraint on the floor role when the answer is 'floor plus a base'. The predicate therefore also admits one-piece OpenLOCK tiles, which already carry their own base. Measured on the floor guide's equivalent set: 128 of 313 otherwise-reachable floors are such tiles.

WHY IT IS NOT CAUGHT BY LOOKING AT THE PAGE: the recommendation is safe. Every size x texture pair resolves to an openforge tile, because connection|openforge sits in the role's 'prefer' list and wins. So the guide looks correct in every default state.

THE FAILURE IS IN THE BROWSE DIALOG, which opens on the role's composed predicate rather than on the recommendation. A person who opens it and picks an OpenLOCK tile gets a parts list showing that tile with a separate base underneath it. The two do not physically go together - the tile is already a base. Nothing tells them.

FIX, one line per with-base option:
    floor:
      require:
        - connection|openforge
PR #253 does exactly this for the floor guide and it costs nothing: with-base then requires openforge, single-piece already denies it, which also makes connection|openforge redundant in the role's 'prefer' list (removed there for the same reason).

Check the wall role too - whether a wall option has the same shape of hole is not something #253 measured.

THE RULE, from Devon 2026-09-30: 'we should keep the floor and wall's connector fixed, *if* it is openforge, or make it !openforge if it isn't. essentially as built it's countermanding the choice for single part print or not.'

The connector on the floor and the wall is not a preference. It is how the print choice is recorded in the data: an openforge tile is bare and needs a base under it, anything else carries its own. So the dialog must never offer a part whose connector disagrees with the answer already given, and the constraint has to be part of the predicate the dialog opens on rather than something the recommendation happens to satisfy.

MEASURED against production, wall guide, separate-wall at 2x2, reading the query each role hands the dialog:

    wall-print=with-base     wall   require [connection|openforge, connection|side|openlock]   deny []
                             floor  require []                                                 deny []
    wall-print=single-piece  wall   require [connection|side|openlock, connection|openlock]     deny [connection|openforge]
                             floor  require [connection|openlock]                               deny [connection|openforge]

So single-piece already does the right thing on both roles - it denies openforge, which is the '!openforge' half of the rule. The gap is entirely on the with-base side, and specifically on the FLOOR: it carries no connector term at all, so the dialog will offer one-piece OpenLOCK floors, which already have their base, while the parts list draws a separate floor-base underneath.

The wall is already correct under with-base because its own option requires openforge.

FIX: floor-print's with-base option needs floor: {require: [connection|openforge]}. That is exactly what the floor guide does - openforge_catalog-yfl added it there for this reason - so this is bringing wall.yaml into line with a fix already shipped and verified elsewhere.

Worth noting what is NOT wrong here: relaxable is only ['texture|...'] in every case, so the browse dialog is not relaxing the connector. The constraint was simply never written for this branch.

title: [scanner] Three trap files have no connection segment and fail to parse
description:
parse_filename requires a connection as the last dot-separated segment and asserts if there is none. These three files have no connection:

  tiles/dungeon_stone/wall_on_tile/wall+special/traps/dungeon_stone#wall,trap+top+axe.2x.stl
  tiles/dungeon_stone/wall_on_tile/wall+special/traps/dungeon_stone#wall,trap+top+dart_holes.2x.stl
  tiles/dungeon_stone/wall_on_tile/wall+special/traps/dungeon_stone#wall,trap+top+magnetic_hole.2x.stl

The scanner writes 'Can't parse: <name>' to stderr and re-raises, so during a full scan this is visible but easy to lose in the output.

Either the files want a connection in their names, or trap tops are a shape that legitimately has none and the parser should say so rather than assert.

Found 2026-09-21 while re-parsing every wall to measure the component|wall fixes.
close_reason: Devon renamed the files 2026-09-21 so they carry a connection segment. Takes effect in the catalog on the next scan; not verifiable from here, since the source files are in Dropbox.

title: [test] Three route tests justify their fixture shape by a claim about wall.yaml that nothing checks
description:
`tests/test_guides_routes.py` around lines 830, 2245 and 2633 justify the shape of the handmade `WALL_GUIDE` dict by asserting in a comment that `openforge/db/fixtures/guides/wall.yaml` ships that shape. Nothing verifies the claim.

If the shipped fixture drifts — a role renamed, a step reordered, a method dropped — those tests stay green while the reason they are written that way quietly stops being true. The failure is not a broken test; it is three tests that still pass and no longer test what their comments say they test.

Found by test-coverage-reviewer in round 3 of PR #246 while enumerating what the shipped fixture has no coverage for. Correctly routed away from that PR as comment rot rather than a coverage gap.

Two possible shapes, neither obviously right: assert the specific correspondence the comments claim (brittle — it pins the fixture's editorial content), or rewrite the comments to stop claiming it and say instead why the handmade shape is a reasonable stand-in. The second is probably correct and is a comment-analyzer job.
notes: Miscited as `openforge_catalog-cvo` in the round-3 commit message on PR #246. That id does not exist — I wrote it without reading the created bead back, which is the one rule I have written down about beads: ids are assigned, not chosen. The correct id is this one, `openforge_catalog-3bc`. The squash message at merge will carry the right one; the intermediate commit will not.

title: Staging runs January code: the workflow never updates the Lambda
description:
CORRECTED. The first version of this bead said staging could not reach the database because a literal PGPASSWORD had gone stale against a rotated secret. That was wrong on every count and is retracted below.

WHAT IS VERIFIED

The staging Lambda (Openforge-Catalog-API, account 682033461796) was last modified 2026-01-01. .github/workflows/staging.yaml builds the API image and pushes it to ECR tagged with the SHA, and stops there: nothing calls update-function-code. The image for 474efe2 is in ECR, unused.

The frontend job in the same workflow DOES deploy. So every merge to test puts a current site on staging.openforge.tools in front of a January backend.

Consequence, confirmed by request: GET /api/guides returns 404 on staging, because the guides routes landed in PR #240 in September. The Guided Builds tab that merge #246 just shipped to staging cannot work there. Staging cannot validate any backend change and has not been able to for nine months.

WHAT IS RETRACTED

Staging can reach the database. POST /api/blueprints/tags returns HTTP 200, 38757 bytes, in 0.62s.

Nothing rotated. The Lambda env PGPASSWORD is sha256 5e9e384c..., byte-identical to the current value in the RDS-managed secret rds!cluster-ff606ebe-381d-4b55-90e4-4b58355be849 and to the one in the bastion bin/.env.

The 502 that started this was GET /api/blueprints, which also returns 502 on production. It is a route the frontend never calls bare; the failure signature is RuntimeError: Failed to post invocation response with no timeout and no OOM, i.e. a response too large for the 1 MB cap on an ALB-invoked Lambda. Filed separately.

THE FIX

Add an image update to staging.yaml after the ECR push, so the deploy deploys:
  aws lambda update-function-code --function-name Openforge-Catalog-API --image-uri <repo>:$GITHUB_SHA
and wait for it to settle before declaring success.

WORTH DOING WHILE IN THERE, NOT URGENT

The env carries a literal PGPASSWORD rather than DB_SECRET_ARN like production, so the next rotation does break it. Switching needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the Lambda role plus a VPC path to Secrets Manager; _password_from_secret fails fast at 3s without one.

The logs carry intermittent "error connecting in pool-1: connection timeout expired". Unproven, but Aurora here is Serverless v2 with MinCapacity 0 and SecondsUntilAutoPause 3600, so a request against a paused cluster is the obvious candidate. It serves fine warm.

Staging Lambda and ALB are still hand-built, not under tofu. This is the argument for finishing that.
notes: WORDING CORRECTION 2026-09-28: where this mentions private subnets as the reason CI cannot reach the database, see openforge_catalog-44e — staging is the default VPC, all six subnets are public, and the barriers are the database security group plus the lack of a NAT. Conclusion unchanged.
close_reason: Superseded by openforge_catalog-9xz / PR #248, which brings staging under tofu and adds the missing image deploy rather than bolting update-function-code onto the old workflow.

title: [api] _get_signed_urls builds a new boto3 S3 client per request, and that is most of the download redirect's warm latency
description:
Found by serverless-architecture-reviewer during review of PR #251 (download-all abort fix), measured against production 2026-09-29.

openforge/app/routes/blueprints.py:174 constructs boto3.client('s3', ...) inside _get_signed_urls, so every call to it pays a fresh botocore service-model load. At 128 MB that load is most of the measured 0.24-0.60 s warm response for GET /api/blueprints/<id>/download.

A module-level client roughly halves the warm response. The client is stateless for presigning and thread-safe for this use, and the credentials come from config that does not change within a container's life.

Why it is worth doing beyond tidiness: the download redirect is on a user-facing critical path that a patron already complained about (openforge_catalog-m8i, ripsnail in New Zealand). Halving it helps most exactly the distant and cellular users who felt the original bug, and it is a single-line change on a cost-conscious 128 MB Lambda.

Note the presign itself is offline HMAC and costs nothing: openforge_catalog-599 establishes the Lambda has no egress at all and presigning still works, so there is no R2 round trip to blame.

Related: openforge_catalog-gvw (128 MB memory sizing) - more memory would also cut the service-model load, but this avoids needing it.

title: [openforge-infra] Staging has no openforge-catalog deploy role and no Secrets Manager endpoint
description:
Blocks openforge_catalog-9xz. Two gaps in terraform/environments/staging, both one-liners, both in openforge-infra.

1. variables.tf deploy_roles defaults to { autoblender = "devonjones/autoblender" } only. Production has openforge-catalog. So staging has no github-actions-openforge-catalog role, which is why staging.yaml authenticates as the raw github_oidc role, whose only permissions are ECRAccess and the website bucket. Add:
     openforge-catalog = "MasterworkTools/openforge-catalog"
   The module then mints the role with PowerUserAccess plus IAM scoped to openforge-catalog-*, the deploy boundary and the state guard, exactly as production.

2. module "network" in staging does not set secretsmanager_endpoint = true; production does, with the comment that the catalog Lambda reads its DB password at cold start. Without the interface endpoint the staging Lambda cannot read DB_SECRET_ARN from the private subnets, and _password_from_secret fails fast at 3s by design.

CAUTION, unrelated drift in the same file: module "database" declares min_capacity = 0.5 and the live cluster reports MinCapacity 0.0. Applying this PR as-is therefore raises the staging floor from zero to 0.5 ACU and starts charging continuously for an environment that idles. Decide deliberately: either set min_capacity = 0 to match reality, or accept the cost. Do not let it ride along unnoticed.

After the apply, set the repo GitHub secret AWS_ROLE_ARN_STAGING to the new deploy role arn.
notes:
WORDING CORRECTION 2026-09-28: this ticket says the Lambda "cannot read DB_SECRET_ARN from the private subnets". The conclusion is right and the mechanism is not. Staging is the **default VPC** — all six subnets are MapPublicIpOnLaunch=true, so they are not private. What actually blocks the call is that there is no NAT and Lambda ENIs get no public IP, so a VPC-attached function has no route to the internet and needs the interface endpoint. Aurora is likewise reachable only from inside the VPC because its security group admits the application and bastion groups and nothing else, not because of subnet privacy.

title: Give the tofu plan jobs a read-only role instead of the PowerUser deploy role
description:
`Staging Plan` and `Production Plan` assume the per-app deploy role, which openforge-infra attaches `PowerUserAccess` to. Both run `tofu plan` over the *pull request head* checkout, on a repository that is public, and both environments have `protection_rules: []` (`production` itself carries a `branch_policy`; the two plan environments carry nothing).

So PR-authored `.tf` — a `data` source, an `external` provider — executes at plan time with credentials that can read Secrets Manager, and the plan output is posted to a public PR. The deploy boundary strips only `iam:*`, `organizations:*` and `account:*` plus write denies on the baseline state prefixes; nothing restricts `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`.

Bounded, not open: fork PRs get no secrets, so this needs push access. Which makes it an insider/compromised-token concern rather than a drive-by one.

Partly mitigated in PR #248 by scoping `Staging Plan` to PRs that touch `terraform/**` or the staging workflows, so unrelated feature PRs no longer hand a runner the role for nothing. `Production Plan` still runs on every PR into main, though those are rare release PRs.

The fix is a second role per app — `github-actions-<app>-plan` — with ReadOnlyAccess plus the state bucket/lock access a plan needs (s3:GetObject on its own prefix, and dynamodb on the lock table if the plan takes one; the plan jobs already pass `-lock=false`, so possibly not even that). Then point both plan workflows at it and leave the deploy role to the apply jobs.

Raised by the credentials-hygiene reviewer on PR #248 as P3; reclassified P2 because that PR widened the trigger from rare release PRs to every feature PR. Wants an openforge-infra change, so it is not a PR #248 fix.

title: The test suite depends on whether the developer has a .env, via LOG_LEVEL
description:
openforge/app/__init__.py calls load_dotenv(), so importing the app puts .env into os.environ. A developer .env with LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG therefore lands in the environment mid-suite, and openforge/db/__init__.py db_url() applies it as a side effect of building a URL:

    if "LOG_LEVEL" in vars:
        LOGGER.setLevel(vars["LOG_LEVEL"])

So the FIRST PgDB(os.environ) built after the app has loaded .env pins the openforge.db logger at DEBUG for the rest of the pytest session. Nothing restores it.

What that breaks, from two files away: tests/test_tags_sql.py::test_a_query_is_not_rendered_when_nothing_is_listening gates on the effective level, and caplog.at_level(WARNING) sets the ROOT level, which cannot mask a level set on the logger itself. The query renders, and the test fails with assert 1 == 0 and DEBUG:openforge.db:rendered in captured stderr.

.env is gitignored, so CI has no LOG_LEVEL and the suite is green there. It fails only on a machine that has one. Found when tests/test_migrate_handler.py became the first test to build a PgDB after app import; worked around there with an autouse fixture that restores the level, but the trap is still armed for the next such test.

Two candidate fixes:
- have db_url stop setting a logger level as a side effect of formatting a URL, and set it once at application startup instead (openforge/app/__init__.py already does exactly that for app.logger)
- or pin the level in tests/conftest.py so the suite does not inherit the developer environment at all

The second is cheaper and closes the class; the first is the actual design problem.

title: [db] The pool opens four Lambda connections and uses one
description:
openforge/db/__init__.py:17 constructs ConnectionPool(self.database_url, open=True). psycopg_pool 3.3.0 defaults to min_size=4, and open=True fills to min_size at construction. Lambda serves one request per container at a time, so a warm container holds four connections open from cold start and can never use more than one of them.

On serverless Postgres, where the connection count is the scarce resource and the cap is hard, that reaches the limit at a quarter of the container count it should. Setting min_size=1 is the whole fix.

Found by the resource-leak-reviewer on PR #240, which it cleared otherwise: it measured that the abort() 404 path does not churn connections (20 consecutive NotFound raised inside pool.connection() left the pool at 2 of 2 available, because psycopg3's Connection.__exit__ skips close() when _pool is set). It deliberately did not post this one, because the line is not in that PR's diff.

Related: openforge_catalog-gvw (Lambda memory) and openforge_catalog-nhf (the loader's full-catalog fetch) are the other two serverless-sizing items.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-09-29 by serverless-architecture-reviewer during review of PR #251 (download-all abort fix), which gives this ticket a concrete multiplier and a new reason to care.

openforge/db/__init__.py:17 is ConnectionPool(url, open=True). psycopg_pool 3.3.0 defaults, read from the signature: min_size=4, max_size=None (which resolves to 4), opened eagerly at container init. max_idle only reaps connections ABOVE min_size, so the four are held for the container's whole life. Lambda serves one request per container at a time, so three of every four sessions are permanently idle.

So the real Aurora cost is 4x the request concurrency, not 1x. reserved_concurrent_executions = 50 means 200 sessions at steady state, not burst.

WHY IT NOW MATTERS MORE: PR #251 removed a pre-flight fetch from downloadFiles, which had been serialising Download-all and holding request concurrency near 1. A Download-all of N files is now N simultaneous requests, hence up to N*4 Aurora sessions. Measured clean at 12 and 25 concurrent against production (302 on every one, zero 5xx), so this is a ceiling rather than a live failure.

THE LEVER: min_size=1, max_size=2 is one kwarg and takes 4x off the scarcest resource. That is the FIRST thing to change if download fan-out or general traffic ever presses on Aurora — ahead of spacing the downloads out client-side, which is what src/utils/blueprint-utils.ts currently names in its ponytail: comment. That comment has been corrected to point here.

Related: openforge_catalog-ot7 (bump psycopg-pool to 3.3.2) touches the same construction and could carry this change.

title: [tests] Nothing resolves a shipped guide against a real catalog
description:
Found by the test-coverage reviewer on PR #253. Predates that PR and applies to both guides.

WHAT IS COVERED TODAY: tests/test_guides_validation.py enumerates openforge/db/fixtures/guides/ rather than naming wall.yaml, so every shipped fixture is schema-validated, and is asserted to carry a hero_image and a summary. Its docstring even anticipates a second guide. CI runs it (pytest tests/ with a postgres service), so a malformed guide DOES fail CI. That part is fine and no per-guide test should be added.

THE GAP: nothing checks that a shipped guide RESOLVES. A schema-valid guide can name a predicate that matches nothing, and the result is the page rendering 'Nothing in the catalog matches this combination yet' - which is exactly what a patron hit on the wall guide, and what openforge_catalog-ume shows is still reachable there today via the rough_stone choice on two methods.

It tests the engine well and cannot test whether a role's predicate matches anything Devon actually modelled.

WHERE IT BELONGS: integration_tests/, which already has a live Flask and the populated dev database. It currently has ZERO guide coverage - grep -rn guide integration_tests/ returns nothing across all nine files.

SHAPE: enumerate the guides from the fixture directory rather than listing them, walk each guide's step options and refinement choices, resolve each combination, and assert no role comes back empty. On the floor guide that is 16 size x print combinations, or 80 with textures; it caught nothing on #253 because it was run by hand, which is the point - nothing would catch it regressing.

title: Tag search inlines every tag as sql.Literal, so 75% of DB time is query planning
description:
Measured by serverless-architecture-reviewer in round 6 of PR #241 (thread 4114300287), against the dev catalog (8,394 blueprints / 81,923 tags) with the real wall.yaml, using EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on every statement each request issues:

  /resolve       4 candidate searches: 557ms planning / 74ms execution
  /availability  48 existence checks: 4413ms planning / 1597ms execution
  /api/tags/query (part dialog) 5 searches: 505ms planning / 177ms execution

Nothing is ever reused: tag values arrive as sql.Literal, so 48 existence checks are 48 distinct statement texts and Postgres parses and plans each from scratch. It worsens with guide depth because _query_tags_basics emits one tag self-join per require, one NOT IN per deny, one NOT EXISTS per deny_children: floor 7.7ms plan / 21.5ms exec, floor-base 196.3ms plan / 2.6ms exec (75x). from_collapse_limit/join_collapse_limit default to 8 and floor-base has ~11 joins, so the planner goes exhaustive.

Fix: bind tag values as parameters instead of inlining literals. Masking literals, the 48 checks are 18 distinct shapes, the two hottest occurring 11 and 10 times within one request. psycopg3 auto-prepares past prepare_threshold=5 and prepared statements live on the pooled connection, so a warm container plans each shape once. sql.Literal is CLAUDE.md's rule against string interpolation, not against bound parameters. Watch the generic-plan risk; plan_cache_mode is the knob. Bigger structural alternative: tag = ANY(%s) ... HAVING count(DISTINCT tag) = %s.

Distinct from openforge_catalog-lrk, which covers HOW MANY queries availability runs. This is what each one costs, and it is the larger factor: halving the checks still leaves ~70% of the remainder in the planner.

Pre-existing (sql.Literal predates the guides work), so not fixed in PR #241. PR #241 did remove 2 of the 62 statements by dropping facets/combinations from the availability call, which fed only a discarded choices list.
notes:
2026-09-28, measured while looking at why the guides' last click is slow. **This ticket is the root cause of `openforge_catalog-lrk`, and the effect is larger than the 75% recorded here.**

Same predicate through `tag_search_blueprints`, ten times in one connection:

    166 167 153 150 155 149 | 11 10 15 14 ms

It collapses ten-fold on the seventh call, which is psycopg3's `prepare_threshold` (5) kicking in and Postgres switching to a cached generic plan. So roughly **92% of that query is planning**, not data work.

In production that never happens, because the 33 `sql.Literal` inlines mean every distinct predicate is a distinct SQL *text*. The guide engine asks a different predicate almost every time, so nothing is ever reused and every query pays full planning cost.

For contrast, the data work really is cheap: a full tag histogram over the whole live catalog — 81,923 tag rows, 900 distinct tags — is 153ms unscoped, and the GIN index on `tags.tag` plus the btree on `(blueprint_id, tag)` are the right shape for this.

Devon's read was that Postgres can run this tag work efficiently. It can. The query layer is what stops it.

Consequence for `-lrk`: the availability sweep issues tens of these per request (30 probes across four roles measured at 2424ms, ~80ms each). Parameterising the predicate so one plan serves every shape would take that to roughly a tenth without changing a single semantic. That is a better first move than bounding `_blame`, because it speeds up the sweep *and* blame *and* every other tag search in the app.

title: Epic: guided builds derive from the catalog instead of hard-coding
description:
An arc, not a single fix. Four tickets share one root cause: the guides hard-code answers and recommendations that the catalog already knows, so the guide goes stale the moment the catalog moves, and nothing fails loudly when it does.

Each one was found the same way - something was scanned, imported and correct, and the guide either could not offer it or recommended something that does not exist.

MEMBERS

  openforge_catalog-g1g  texture lists are hand-curated, so a scanned texture is invisible until
                         someone edits two fixtures. This is the root: nova_trail shipped and could
                         not be picked, and answering with it was a 400.

  openforge_catalog-f8l  the base-clips DEFAULT is a fixed string naming magnets + OpenLOCK +
                         topless. Zero bases carry that at one inch, because magnets and OpenLOCK
                         do not fit on the same face at that size, so a 1x1 build resolves to
                         nothing while 47 usable one-inch wall bases sit there. The ANSWERS derive
                         correctly; only the default does not.

  openforge_catalog-xkd  the floor texture default is a hand-written clause list. Devon's spec:
                         config if it names one and it exists, else the same top level texture if
                         it exists, else dungeon stone block. Cannot pair with a derived list.

  openforge_catalog-y8m  per-face connectors are not modelled at all. The dual/triplex bases are
                         one part with different connectors on different faces, and the tag
                         vocabulary is per part, so 'magnets on the floor joints, none toward the
                         wall' is not expressible. Hardest of the four: the others need existing
                         facts derived, this needs the facts recorded first.

THE SHARED SHAPE. Where the engine derives, it is right - base-clips narrows its offered combinations per size, and the texture question narrows per build. Every failure here is a place where a curated list or a fixed default sits beside that machinery and does not use it.

SUGGESTED ORDER. g1g first, since it is the root and the pattern the rest copy. f8l next and small - the derivation already exists, the default just has to use it. xkd depends on g1g being done, or the mapping cannot be data alongside a derived list. y8m last and largest, since it needs a modelling decision before any derivation is possible.

ALSO IN THE FAMILY, not blocked by this: openforge_catalog-ume, the hand-written texture counts that are all wrong. g1g deletes that problem rather than fixing it, since a derived list carries its own count.

title: [guides] Clicking an answer gives no sign it registered
description:
DrTorte, 2026-09-30, on the guided builds release: 'Some kind of UI indication that it's responding to your clicks would be great, I'm sometimes not sure if my click got registered or not. It's only really noticeable when you click on the textures though.'

Devon: 'I'll see what I can do about making that it's working clearer. I have some performance work to do here, but I wanted to get it functioning first.'

WHY TEXTURES SPECIFICALLY: answering a question re-resolves the whole build - every in-play role is recomposed and re-queried - and the page shows the old answer until the new parts come back. Texture is the question where that gap is most visible, because it is usually answered late, when every role is in play and each one costs a catalog round trip.

TWO SEPARATE THINGS, worth not conflating:

1. Feedback. The click should show immediately that it was received - the chip taking a selected state on click rather than when the response lands, and the parts area showing it is refreshing. That is a frontend change alone and does not depend on anything getting faster.

2. Latency. The resolve behind it is genuinely slow. Related and already filed: openforge_catalog-lrk (the availability endpoint costs a second Lambda invocation and ~2.4s), openforge_catalog-43f (a boto3 client is built per request, which is most of the download redirect's warm latency), openforge_catalog-gvw (128 MB Lambda sizing).

Do 1 regardless of 2. A click that visibly registers is worth more than a faster click that still looks dead.

title: Scanner: floor shapes nest under shape|floor

title: validate_schema re-parses YAML on every request; caching it needs a deepcopy
description:
Found by serverless-architecture-reviewer in round 8 of PR #241, pre-existing.

validate_schema() as openforge/app/routes/tags.py:69 calls it costs 4.1 ms per request, and 3.65 ms of that (89%) is re-parsing the YAML off the Lambda filesystem. Nothing about it is request-specific, and it is on the catalog's main search endpoint. deepcopy of the already-parsed dict is 38 us -- 96x cheaper.

THE TRAP, which is why this must not be done casually: a plain @lru_cache on load_schema is a SILENT VALIDATION HOLE. validate_schema(..., required=False) MUTATES the dict it was handed (schema["required"] = []), and /api/images and /api/tag_descriptions both mix required=False and required=True calls within one warm container. Caching the parse without deepcopying the result would let a required=False call permanently strip the required list for every later required=True call on the same container -- validation silently weakened, no error, no log.

So the fix is: cache the parse, deepcopy on every return. The deepcopy is what makes it safe, not an optimisation to skip.

Note the guide endpoints do no per-request schema validation at all (guide.yaml is fixture-load only), so this is confined to the tags endpoints.

title: [guides] Back reloads the page when a blueprint is selected and a guide created a history entry
description:
`use-blueprint-url-cleanup.ts:33-40` reloads on **any** `popstate` when a blueprint is selected and the URL has no `blueprint_id` — and lines 23-31 of the same hook strip `blueprint_id` as soon as a blueprint is selected, so that condition is permanently true once someone clicks a result.

Nothing created history entries on `/` before, so it never fired there. PR #246's `selectGuide` uses `pushState` (so Back returns to the cards), which now gives it something to fire on.

Reproduced by in-tab-reviewer: select a result row in Part Search, switch to Guided Builds, click the Wall card, press Back → a document `load` for `/`, active tab back to Part Search, blueprint selection gone. Control with no blueprint selected: no load event, Back lands on the cards, the tab stays.

Not fixed in #246, deliberately. The two candidate fixes both reach outside that PR's scope:

1. **Narrow the hook to what it means.** Its intent is 'backing out of a blueprint deep link resets the selection', so it should reload only when the selection *came from* the URL. That is a ref set when the hook actually strips a `blueprint_id`. It changes blueprint behaviour, and `use-blueprint-url-cleanup.test.ts:134` asserts the blunt rule directly (`search: ''`, no `blueprint_id` ever present, expects a reload), so that test encodes the thing to change.
2. **Drop `pushState` from `selectGuide`.** Sidesteps it entirely and costs Back-returning-to-the-cards, which is a real part of the tab feeling like a tab.

Option 1 is better and is a blueprint-side change. Worth doing with the blueprint flow in front of you rather than inside a guides page redesign.

title: Guided builds: offer a plain base as an alternative to the wall base
description:
Requested by ripsnail on 2026-09-29: "Would be handy if there was extra option under Other options to switch the wall base out for a plain base as well. I personally have been using the dual bases a bunch. Although maybe that is just me."

The wall guide currently resolves the wall-base role to a wall-specific base (e.g. dungeon_stone#base+wall.A.openlock+topless,magnetic+flex.stl). They want to swap that for a plain base — the same piece the floor-base role already resolves to (plain#base+square.2x2.openlock+topless,magnetic+flex.stl) — so both roles can use the dual bases they prefer.

Shape of the change: a refinement under Other options, scoped to the wall-base role, toggling between the wall-specific base and the plain one. The parts already exist in the catalog and the floor-base role already selects the plain variant, so this is a guide-document and refinement question rather than new data.

Worth checking whether the part-selection modal already permits this by hand (open the wall base, relax the shape|base|wall restriction, pick the plain one). If it does, the request is really "make the thing I can already do discoverable", which is a smaller change and argues for a refinement rather than new machinery.

title: [guided builds] Resolution engine in Python
description: Pure function: guide document plus a selection map in, resolved parts and the steps now reachable out. No HTTP, no database access in the core — candidate lookup is injected so the engine stays testable. src/CLAUDE.md is explicit that real logic belongs in Python, and this is real logic. Three things settled during design review: (1) the recommendation must be deterministic or the shareable URL does not reproduce what the person saw — the separate-wall wall role leaves 2,278 candidates on the literal query and 1,221 once prefer:connection|openforge is applied, and that prefer list ranks none of those 1,221 above another, so extend prefer until it totally orders and state the final tie-break (blueprint_name is the existing sort and the obvious one); (2) guides do NOT use constrain — it has no Python implementation, its real semantics include parent:false, siblings and filter-as-exclusion, and the thing it buys (every role the same size) is better asked than inferred, so size is a step and every role's composed query requires the chosen size|width|* outright; (3) composition rule: the composed query is the union of the method's tags, the role's query and any active refinements, each predicate list concatenated, with deny beating require — the engine knows nothing about the 177 dual-shape (shape|wall + shape|floor) pieces, and a guide that does not want a combined print denies the other shape in that role's query. A role whose composed query matches nothing resolves to no part and says so rather than silently dropping out. Unit tested against the real wall fixture, including options that beget options and options that remove them.

Seven review rounds, 62 findings addressed.

title: Guide: browse and pin a part from the catalog dialog
description: Clicking a part in a guide opens the tag search. It should (a) seed from a relaxed predicate so people can browse the obscure options - keep the role sweep, method, print style, tile size and side clips; relax wall height, texture, base clips and pegs; (b) open straight onto the blueprint the guide currently recommends, as an option so other callers are unaffected; (c) let 'select this part' pin that blueprint to the role, replacing the recommendation, shown as a user selection with a way to clear it.
close_reason: Closed

title: [guides] selectGuide pushes a history entry even when the URL is unchanged
description:
`selectGuide(key)` always `pushState`s, so clicking a control that resolves to the URL you are already on adds a dead history entry — Back then does nothing visible for one press.

Measured by general-reviewer in round 4 of PR #246: `history.length` 7 -> 9 over two such clicks, with Back dead twice.

The reachable case in #246 was 'Start this guide over' on the error arm, where the URL already is `?guide=<key>`. That control no longer intercepts, so the symptom is gone — but the cause is still in `selectGuide`, and any future caller that lands on the current URL will reproduce it.

Fix belongs in `selectGuide` rather than at the call sites: compare the composed search string against `window.location.search` and return early when they match, rather than asking every caller to know whether it is a no-op. `clearGuide` has the same shape — calling it from the cards, where there is no guide to clear, pushes an entry for nothing.

Not done in #246, which is a page redesign; it is small enough to fold into the `openforge_catalog-lrk` engine work, where the URL and resolution paths are being looked at anyway.

title: Propagate thingiverse sync data to AWS prod (fixture + API upsert path)
description: The tool runs against the LOCAL Postgres, but prod (AWS Lambda + serverless Postgres) is populated by replaying fixture JSON through the Flask API (bin/upload_fixture with OPENFORGE_BASE_URL, same pattern as blueprint fixtures). Thingiverse data (blueprint_id <-> thing_id mapping, public thing URLs) must ride that path so the app can render Thingiverse links in prod and support deeper integration later. Deliverables: fixture format for thingiverse mappings (exported from the local sync tables), an authenticated API upsert endpoint in the Flask app, and upload_fixture support. Note: prod likely only needs the mapping/links, not the per-file hash ledger — that is local operational state; decide the split when designing the fixture.
notes: DESIGN NOTE from PR #225 review: the schema allows one blueprint to appear in MULTIPLE things (partial unique index is per-thing only, and test_same_source_allowed_in_different_things pins that behavior). The prod fixture mapping is therefore 1:N — (blueprint_id, thing_id, public_url) derived per thingiverse_files row, not a unique-per-blueprint map. The app's Thingiverse links UI must handle a blueprint linking to several things.

title: [guided builds] guides table, fixture format and loader
description: New schema version: a guides table holding the guide document as jsonb keyed by a short key. Fixture format is YAML in openforge/db/fixtures/guides/, loaded by the existing fixtures command the way tag_descriptions is, with an OpenAPI schema beside the others in openforge/openapi/schemas/ so a malformed guide fails loudly and names the offending step. See docs/design/guided-builds.md for the document shape: steps with options, roles with tag queries and a prefer list, refinements with a declarative when: predicate over earlier selections.
notes: Reconciled with 'fulfills' rather than inventing a parallel mechanism. 'fulfills' is used 41 times in two positions that mean different things: 21 at the root of a blueprint (7 in cut-stone.json, 14 in dungeon_stone.json) saying this whole piece satisfies a slot of that name, and 20 entries across 18 of the s2w composition blueprints saying one part satisfies a sibling part's slot — the wall that is its own base. The guide format expresses the second without a new mechanism: an option lists the roles its build needs, so a method whose wall is its own base simply does not list the base role. The declarative when: predicate covers the options-beget-options half. Decided while implementing: option.roles is a map of role name to predicate (null for none) rather than a list, because a method is not one tag — the composites put build|s2w on the floor, build|separate wall on the wall and deny build|s2w on the base; option.tags remains as the shorthand for what is true of every role the option names. Toggle refinements are spelled on_tags/off_tags because bare on/off are YAML 1.1 booleans.

Seven review rounds, 62 findings addressed.

title: [guides] The floor guide reaches 313 of 533 floors; 73 are unreachable by any answer or browse
description:
Measured 2026-09-29 by the guide-semantics reviewer on PR #253, against the floor role's own set of 533 plain floors.

    313  reachable by answering (8 sizes x 5 textures)
    147  unreachable by answering, RECOVERABLE by browsing (texture is browsable)
     73  unreachable by ANY route
    ---
    533  total

CORRECTION 2026-09-29: the middle figure was first recorded as 165 and the three did not
add up - 313+165+73 = 551 against a role set of 533. 165 is a different quantity: the
floors whose texture is none of the five offered, AT ANY SIZE (533-368). 18 of those also
have an unoffered footprint, so they are already counted in the 73 and browsing cannot
recover them, because texture is browsable and size is not. The browse-recoverable figure
is 147, which is also what the arithmetic forces once 533, 313 and 73 are each confirmed.

The 73 are the ones that matter. Their footprint is not one of the eight the size step offers, and because that step is not browsable its tags never enter 'relaxable' - so neither answering nor the catalog dialog reaches them:

    6x4 (17), 6x6 (15), 8x8 (15)  - 45 of these are plain, in cut-stone, dungeon_stone and towne.
                                    cut-stone#floor.6x6.openforge.stl and
                                    dungeon_stone%block#floor.8x8.openforge.stl cannot be produced at all.
    the rest at odd and transposed pairs. Measured histogram of all 73:
        6x4 17, 6x6 15, 8x8 15, 1x2 4, 3x2 4, 2x4 4,
        and 2 each at 8x2, 3x4, 1x3, 4x3, 1x4, 6x2, 2x3.
    (An earlier version of this note grouped these as "6x2, 8x2, 3x2, 1x2 (8)" and
    "22 more at transposed/odd pairs"; those measure 12 and 14. The total of 73 was right.)
    The celtic-knot straight runner is designed across 1x2/2x1/2x2/3x2/4x2/6x2/8x2 and the
    guide reaches three of seven.

63 of the 73 are undecorated, so this is not a long tail of oddities.

This is openforge_catalog-p1h relocated: there the unreachability was in the role predicate, here it is in the answer list.

NOT A ONE-LINE FIX. 6x4 and 8x8 have no square base at all, so offering them would empty floor-base on the with-base branch - trading an unreachable piece for a dead end, which is the failure mode this project already hit. Options, roughly in order of cost: offer the extra sizes only on the single-piece branch (no base needed); make size browsable and accept that a browsed size may empty the base; or model the missing bases.

SEPARATELY, the 165: the texture choices offer five tags, and cave (46 floors) is larger than aztlan (24), which has a button. streets 29, cavern 16, dwarven_halls 16, large_brick 16, pool 16, sewer 10, cracked_ice 8, necro 8. They are reachable by browsing, so this is a discoverability question rather than a correctness one - but a floor guide that cannot offer cave floors by name is worth a second look. Deliberately not changed in #253, which was scoped to mirroring the wall guide.

title: [loader] The fixture summary counts deprecation candidates, not deprecations applied
description:
Loading the regenerated aztlan fixture after the separate_walls -> separate_wall rename printed:

  aztlan.json: Applied 236 added, 3 modified, 236 deprecated

Nothing was deprecated. The database afterwards has 289 live aztlan blueprints and zero deprecated ones, 227 of them on the new path. The move handling worked exactly as designed.

The summary is built from len(self.deprecated) (openforge/db/fixtures/incremental.py:84), which is the candidate list produced during comparison. The apply step then skips entries whose id is in _renamed_blueprint_ids (:829) — 'the row was already updated in place, deprecating it now would tombstone the live row' — and the count is never adjusted.

Why it matters more than a cosmetic miscount: a directory rename is exactly when you are least sure you have not broken something, and the run reports having deprecated a quarter of the texture. The honest reading of that output is data loss. Someone seeing it on a bigger rename would reasonably stop and start investigating, or worse, restore from a backup over a database that was fine.

Fix is to count what was applied rather than what was proposed — either decrement as entries are skipped, or report both ('236 proposed, 0 applied, 236 renamed in place'), which is arguably more useful because it says the renames were recognised.

Note the scanner side is separately correct and prints its own DEBUG line for the same files: openforge/data/incremental.py:524 declines to write deprecation tombstones into the fixture when the same MD5 appears elsewhere in the scan. Two layers, both right, and only the summary is wrong.

Found 2026-09-21 verifying the aztlan regeneration end to end.

title: GET /api/blueprints returns 502 in both environments: the response exceeds Lambda's 6 MB limit
description:
GET /api/blueprints returns 502 on production (openforge.tools) and on staging, consistently, in 8-10 seconds.

THE CAP THAT BITES IS LAMBDA 6 MB SYNCHRONOUS RESPONSE LIMIT, not the ALB 1 MB one. This ticket originally said ALB; that was wrong. Measured 2026-09-28 from CloudWatch, 12 occurrences in 60 days, most recent that day:

    LAMBDA_RUNTIME Failed to post handler success response. Http response code: 413.
    RuntimeError: Failed to post invocation response
    Runtime exited with error: exit status 1
    REPORT ... Memory Size: 128 MB  Max Memory Used: 128 MB

413 is the response-size rejection: the runtime built a response it could not return. Not a timeout, not an OOM.

openforge/app/index.py registers the route; openforge/app/routes/blueprints.py:43 get_blueprints() -> get_all_blueprints(cursor) -> jsonify(data) lists every blueprint with no limit and no pagination. 8,721 blueprints (measured; an earlier note in circulation said "roughly 14000", which was the STL file count, not the blueprint count).

Consequence worth stating plainly: raising memory_size cannot fix this. 6 MB is a service limit, so this is a genuinely different problem from openforge_catalog-gvw even though both surface to a user as the same 502.

Priority P2, and the reason it is not lower: a route anyone can reach returns 502 with no traceback, and it is observed rather than projected. It is reached rarely because no frontend caller uses it bare — the UI goes through POST /api/blueprints/tags and the per-id sub-paths — but it is reachable by anyone who guesses the URL, and 12 hits in 60 days says something does.

Options, cheapest first: paginate with a default limit, or drop the GET and keep the POST if nothing needs an unfiltered listing.

Found while probing staging during the #248 deploy, where it sent me down a wrong path: I read its 502 as evidence that staging had lost its database, and it fails identically in production. Diagnosis corrected by the serverless-architecture reviewer in round 2 of that PR.
notes:
MEASURED 2026-09-28 by the serverless-architecture reviewer on PR #248, and the diagnosis in the description is wrong in one detail: the cap that bites is Lambda 6 MB synchronous response limit, not the ALB 1 MB one.

Observed, 12 times in 60 days, most recently 2026-09-28 20:09:

    LAMBDA_RUNTIME Failed to post handler success response. Http response code: 413.
    RuntimeError: Failed to post invocation response
    Runtime exited with error: exit status 1
    REPORT ... Memory Size: 128 MB  Max Memory Used: 128 MB

413 is the response-size rejection. openforge/app/routes/blueprints.py:43 get_blueprints() -> get_all_blueprints(cursor) -> jsonify(data) over 8,721 blueprints, with no limit and no pagination.

Two consequences worth recording. Raising memory_size cannot fix this — 6 MB is a service limit, so this is a separate problem from openforge_catalog-gvw even though both surface as the same 502. And it is pre-existing on the January image, but PR #248 is what finally points staging at current code, so it stops being invisible.

Raised P3 -> P2: a route anyone can reach returns 502 with no traceback, and it is now observed rather than projected.

STILL LIVE 2026-09-29, re-observed incidentally during review of PR #251: production GET /api/blueprints 502s after 7.6 s, and /api/guides answers 200 in 0.29 s.

CORRECTION 2026-09-29: an earlier version of this paragraph reported that "?limit=5 also 502s" and inferred from it that "the handler builds the full result set before applying any limit". The inference was bogus. There IS no limit parameter: get_blueprints (openforge/app/routes/blueprints.py:43) reads no request.args at all, and get_all_blueprints (openforge/db/sql/blueprints.py:48) is a bare SELECT with no LIMIT. So ?limit=5 502s because the parameter is ignored entirely, not because a limit is applied too late. The conclusion — pagination must push the bound into the query — is still right, but it has to be built rather than fixed, and a reader should not go looking for existing pagination to repair.

CONFIRMED A LIVE OUTAGE 2026-09-29, not an intermittent one, by js-async-reviewer during review of PR #251: 502 on 6 of 6 attempts, 8.4-11.6 s each, with and without query params.

Controls that PASS, which localise it to this endpoint rather than the environment:
    POST /api/blueprints/tags      -> 200 in 1.0 s
    GET  /api/blueprints/<uuid>/download -> 404, fast
    GET  /api/guides               -> 200 in 0.29 s

So the Lambda is up and the database is reachable; it is this query and this response. Note 8-11 s is well inside the 30 s Lambda timeout, which is consistent with the 413 response-size rejection already recorded above rather than with a hang.

This is the catalog-list endpoint returning 502 to anyone who calls it, so it is worth treating as more urgent than its P2 suggests if anything in the frontend still calls it.

title: Bring staging under tofu so a merge to test deploys the whole way
description:
Staging predates tofu: its Lambda, ALB, listeners and target groups were hand-built, so staging.yaml can only push an image to ECR and sync a frontend. Mirror terraform/environments/production as terraform/environments/staging and rewire the workflow to docker-build -> tofu-apply -> migrate -> frontend-deploy, so the frontend is never promoted ahead of the backend it needs.

WHAT IMPORTS CLEANLY (names already match production)
- aws_lb.api: openforge-catalog
- aws_lb_target_group.api: openforge-catalog-api (the 80 and 443 listeners both already forward to it)
- aws_lb_listener.http: the port 80 listener, default fixed-response 404, which is exactly what production declares
- aws_lb_listener_rule.api: priority 1, path /api/*
- aws_s3_bucket.site and its website config, public access block and policy: staging-openforge-catalog-website

WHAT CANNOT BE ADOPTED
The function is named Openforge-Catalog-API and its role is Openforge-Catalog-API-role-ogdz6ix0 under the service-role path. The deploy role can only manage IAM named openforge-catalog-*, and function_name is ForceNew, so neither can be imported into the production-shaped resources. Tofu creates openforge-catalog-api, its role, and its log group fresh, and the old pair is deleted by hand after the first apply succeeds (see the cleanup ticket).

DEPENDS ON openforge-infra: staging has no deploy role for this repo at all (deploy_roles is autoblender only), and no Secrets Manager VPC endpoint, which the Lambda needs to read DB_SECRET_ARN at cold start.

PREREQUISITES, once per account
- openforge-catalog/staging/app in Secrets Manager. scripts/create-app-secret.sh generates a FRESH API_TOKEN and SECRET_KEY, which rotates the admin token staging answers to; decide deliberately whether to preserve the current values instead.
- Repo GitHub secret AWS_ROLE_ARN_STAGING = the new deploy role arn.

CloudFront reaches the ALB http-only on port 80, so modelling only the port 80 listener matches reality; the 443 listener is unused.

Supersedes the narrow fix in openforge_catalog-3em.

title: [catalog] Half the walls are not on the unified separate-wall part yet
description:
The wall guide (openforge_catalog-z76) requires build|separate wall on its wall role, because all three build methods now take the same wall part. That unification is real but incomplete across the collection, so the guide can currently reach about half the walls.

Measured 2026-09-21 against the full fixture set, models only, not deprecated:

  668 pieces carry shape|wall + component|wall
  364 carry build|separate wall            (reachable by the guide)
   71 carry build|wall on tile only
   40 carry build|s2w only
  193 carry no build tag at all

The 193 with no build tag are the largest group and probably the ones that have simply not been touched.

The user-visible consequence is in the texture refinement, which is how someone asks for a wall that is not dungeon stone. Openforge component walls by texture, and how many the guide can reach:

  towne             153 -> 100
  dungeon_stone      81 ->  48

title: Sync engine: diff local files vs remote hashes, reconcile
description: For each managed thing: diff manifest-directed local files against remote files by normalized-MD5 comparison (via the thingiverse_files ledger) -> upload new, replace changed, delete removed, patch drifted metadata. Idempotent; dry-run mode showing planned actions before mutating. ALSO IN SCOPE: adopt/backfill existing Thingiverse things into the ledger by matching remote files to catalog blueprints by MD5, so things created outside the tool (or in prior manual runs) are recognized and never duplicated (see NOTES for the proven recipe + open decisions). Remote hash confirmed = content-MD5.
notes:
VALIDATED on real data (thing:7364110): Thingiverse file hash = content-MD5 (NOT SHA-256). Two compare requirements: (1) hash encoding VARIES — old things hex MD5 (32ch), recent base64 MD5 (24ch, e.g. lma97RnU7yEQDMZcDe1vEA==); normalize before compare (24-char/b64 -> decode to hex; 32-char -> lowercase; see client.normalize_hash). (2) Thingiverse SANITIZES filenames on upload (strips #, comma, etc). Match files by MD5, NEVER by name.

ADOPTION (added scope — proven manually 2026-07-08, must be reproduced in ad5):
ad5 must ADOPT existing Thingiverse things into the ledger, not only create new ones — otherwise it will create DUPLICATES of things made outside the tool or in prior runs. Recipe validated on 9 things / 347 links this session:
- GET /users/me/things (newest); select by criterion (published-year / --since date).
- Per thing: get_thing_files -> normalize_hash -> match to blueprints.file_md5 (UNIQUE, so md5->blueprint is 1:1).
- Upsert thingiverse_things (thing_id unique; status from is_published; published_at from `added`; last_synced_at=now) ON CONFLICT (thing_id).
- Rebuild thingiverse_files matched rows (blueprint_id), dedup per (thing, blueprint). Idempotent.
- A blueprint can map to MULTIPLE things (20 shared seen — e.g. bases across releases); per-thing uniqueness only, do NOT assume 1:1.
NOTE: a manual adoption snapshot already exists in the DEV DB only (9 things, 347 links). ad5 adoption must be idempotent so re-running over it is safe.

OPEN DECISIONS ad5 must resolve (the manual one-off punted on these):
- Non-catalog remote files (zips, gallery images): the thingiverse_files CHECK requires blueprint_id|image_id|local_path; an adopted remote-only zip/image has none of these. Either relax the CHECK to allow remote-only rows (remote_file_id set), or track only catalog-matched files. The manual run recorded matched MODEL files ONLY (skipped zips/images).
- remote_metadata_hash baseline for adopted things: left NULL manually; decide compute-from-current-metadata vs NULL.

REAL-RUN LEARNINGS (creating thing:7380581 + adopting 9):
- uploadFile AUTO-CLASSIFIES by mime type: PNG -> gallery image (sets default_image, not in file list); STL/zip -> downloadable file. One upload method for all.
- HARD per-file limit 250 MiB (262144000 bytes): "File is larger than maximum allowed size". ad5 must split oversized bundles (we split a 327MB zip by directory into two sub-250MiB zips) or skip+warn.
- update_thing PATCH accepts `tags` -> tags are patchable/drift-reconcilable (also license/category/description).
- Transient HTTP 500s on large uploads AND 429 rate-limiting both observed: throttle (~3s between calls) + exponential backoff/retry. Old v1 tooling used 3s sleeps.
- Zips are aggregate bundles (file_type=zip, not blueprint-backed).

title: tags endpoint: NUL in a JSON body or a cursor is a 500, not a 400
description:
From round 7 of PR #241 (error-handling-reviewer thread 4115811989, with silent-failure-hunter reaching the same file independently).

POST /api/blueprints/tags still reaches sql.Literal with unvalidated input on several keys, so a hand-crafted NUL in a JSON body is a psycopg DataError and an unhandled 500 rather than a 400:

  {"deny_children": [{"tag": "shape|\u0000wall"}]}   -> 500
  {"require":       [{"tag": "shape|\u0000wall"}]}   -> 500  (pre-existing)
  next=%00, previous=%00, limit=%00                  -> 500  (pre-existing)
  limit=abc, next=notanid                            -> 500  (InvalidTextRepresentation, pre-existing)
  GET /api/blueprints/tags/<tag> with shape%00wall   -> 500  (pre-existing)

{"allow": [...]} alone returns 200, because allow is only read as an exemption when a deny_children is present.

PR #241 closed the neighbouring half: required: [tag] now covers all five predicate terms, so a tagless item is a 400 at the boundary. The NUL case is what is left.

Why it was not fixed in #241: the class is pre-existing across require/deny/accept and the pagination cursors; it is not reachable from the frontend (it needs a hand-written \u0000 in a JSON body); and one `pattern` on the tag string in tag_query.yaml closes all five keys at once, which is a better change than five guards and did not belong at the end of a review round.

The guide endpoints are sealed -- _selections_from_request and _guide_or_404 both guard NUL, verified by probe on both routes.
